docs.title: SYNK — About us
paragraphs: SYNK builds personalized systems. We develop technology that understands each person’s goals, circumstances, and experience and provides the support they need. As their goals and needs change, the system is designed to change with them.

SYNK LAB — Learn Korean and develop your own judgment. LAB aims to prepare learners for studying in Korea and the life that follows. With TOPIK Level 4 as a clear goal, learners also gain experience using Korean in real situations. We want to help people use AI while being able to explain their own thinking and judge the results.

SYNK SHIFT — Learn AI and put it to work. Knowing about AI tools and using them in your work are different things. SHIFT is preparing training and consulting that help participants find approaches suited to their own work by making and reviewing real outputs.

SYNK PULSE — Making time for music and stories. PULSE values the enjoyment of a work and the impression it leaves. Through music, video, and character stories, we want to create work people return to hear and see again.

SYNK PATH — Helping students find their own way in Korean academic and everyday life. PATH aims to help students participate in classes in Korean, solve everyday problems, and make their own career decisions. We are preparing a service that combines study planning around each student’s intended major and career with Korean learning and VR scenario practice. Students’ writing, presentations, and project work are organized into portfolios. Schools and employers can understand their motivation and experience through materials the students agree to share.
Each brand’s website explains which experiences are available now and which services are still in preparation.

Finding a reason to learn, making your own choices, and creating something together. I want technology to make more room for these experiences. That is why I am building SYNK.

The creator introduced on this website and in SHIFT content is the founder. He sets the company’s direction, decides which tasks to delegate to AI and which results to review personally, and shares the actual production process and the reasons for revisions.

Founder Yuho Yang’s education: Department of Architecture, Howon University · Department of Psychology, Chung-Ang University. In his words: “I bring my studies of spaces and people, stage and creative projects, and experience running an educational institution into the planning and making of SYNK.”
Education · Operations — 2026 Former Deputy Director, Skyline Edu, Mongolia (Student advising, class operations, and online promotion)

Performance · Projects — 2023 RCA · Royal College of Art (Royal College of Art graduate project · Main Performer), 2023 TV series “Bora! Deborah” · Netflix (Appearance in the opening sequence of Episode 1), 2014 LOEN Entertainment (Performer)

Studying architecture and psychology, performing on stage, and working in education in Mongolia have each given me a different perspective: an eye for structure, an interest in how people think and act, and experience creating something with others. At SYNK, I bring these perspectives together to design support around each person's goals and circumstances.

Atlas is SYNK's core technology for finding the learning and support each person needs, based on their goals and experience. Eight engines share the work: understanding the person, choosing what to learn and in what order, explaining it, and reviewing the results.

A student may first prepare for university admission, then need help with presentations or job interviews while studying in Korea. We are developing Atlas to adjust tasks and explanations using the learner's new goals and recent work.
Core — Choosing the next learning step. Looks at what a learner wants to achieve and where they are struggling, then identifies the next task and the support they need.
Loom — Scenes that respond to you. Combines soft materials, light, and movement to create interfaces and characters, with scenes that respond naturally to the user's actions.

Vellum — Explanations that make sense. Offers explanations and hints suited to the current task and the student's answer. Explains why the practice matters and what to look at when the student gets stuck.
Trail — Tracking practice and progress. Records the tasks completed and the help received. Lets learners compare earlier and recent answers to see what has changed.
Prism — Comparing learning results. Finds recurring difficulties and differences across learning examples. Highlights which content and explanations need a closer look.
Temper — Checking whether support helped. Checks what actually changed after a hint or practice activity, then uses those results to improve tasks and support.
Reed — Music and sound for each scene. Handles music and sound for creative work and learning scenes. Adjusts their use around the listening experience and moments that need focus.

Strata (planned) — A map of what to learn next. Connects grammar, expressions, and vocabulary by difficulty and prerequisites. Helps identify the learning needed for a goal and which basics to revisit after a mistake.

docs.title: SYNK LAB — Learning
paragraphs: SYNK LAB is an edtech company developing Korean textbooks, learning games, and a personalized learning app. We are preparing a one-year, in-person program targeting TOPIK Level 4, along with conversation classes with native Korean teachers and global English classes. Our approach connects cultural experiences, AI use, and collaborative projects to prepare learners for studying and living in Korea.

Learn Korean and learn to think for yourself. LAB aims to prepare learners for studying in Korea and for life beyond it. TOPIK Level 4 is a clear goal, supported by experience using Korean in real situations. We want to help learners use AI while developing the ability to explain their own thinking and evaluate the results.

We are preparing education for everyone who wants to learn Korean. We look at the Korean learners need in daily life, study, and work, and are developing the curriculum, textbooks, and student app as we prepare to open.

We aim to use learners’ own sentences and choices to inform subsequent tasks and feedback. Participation requirements and schedules will be announced separately for each program. Learning outcomes are not guaranteed.
Edtech for personalized Korean learning

LAB is preparing education for everyone who wants to learn Korean. Eligibility is not limited by nationality or place of residence. We research lessons based on how learners want to use Korean and their current ability.

We are currently developing the curriculum, textbooks, and student app as we prepare to open. Check each online or in-person program’s information for its intended learners, starting level, and participation requirements.

We first explore what learners want to do in Korean and what they find difficult. We are preparing classes in which students use what they have learned in real situations, receive feedback, and practice again in the next task.

Practice includes asking questions in university classes, explaining what you enjoy, and sharing opinions in team activities. We are preparing different ways to participate, including planning and editing as well as speaking and writing.

The classroom scenes on this website are examples explaining our approach. They are not actual student records or verified learning outcomes. Each student’s learning outcomes must be assessed through actual classes and experience.
SYNK LAB’s textbooks comprise six Synapse Core grammar books and two Synapse Talk conversation books—eight in total. The manuscripts are complete, and we are preparing for publication.

The learning goals for each Synapse Core book are:
Book 1 · TOPIK Level 1 — Read Hangul and introduce yourself.
Book 2 · TOPIK Level 2 — Build basic sentence patterns for everyday conversation.
Book 3 · TOPIK Levels 2–3 — Talk naturally about familiar everyday situations.
Book 4 · TOPIK Level 3 — Share your opinion and explain your reasons.
Book 5 · TOPIK Levels 3–4 — Explain your views on social issues.
Book 6 · TOPIK Levels 4–5 — Discuss specialist and abstract topics.

Synapse Talk Book 1 covers beginner conversation and connects with Core Books 1–2. Book 2 covers intermediate conversation and connects with Core Books 3–5. The conversation books cover material through TOPIK Level 4.

The levels indicate each book’s learning goals, not a guarantee of passing. The manuscripts are complete, but final review and publication are still in preparation. Publication dates and access details will be announced separately.
The correction reply screen on this website illustrates a learning app in development. It does not show actual student records or learning outcomes.

In this situation, you ask your professor for an assignment extension. The original sentence, “3일만 더 주세요.” (Please give me just three more days), stays unchanged, and the corrected sentence is recorded separately.

The sample correction is “제출 기한을 3일만 더 연장해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.” (I would appreciate it if you could extend the deadline by just three days). Replies are reviewed by a person and may take several days to arrive.

If you choose to practice again after reading the reply, you try a new task in the next game. Select Original, Correction reply, and Next practice to explore this process. In the email-writing experience currently available, you write and revise your own text without automatic correction.
Use Korean learned from textbooks in games. LAB is developing an app that adjusts subsequent tasks and feedback using students’ answers and the areas where they needed help.

Practice Korean you will use. We turn situations that require Korean—such as writing a request email to a professor—into games. Students choose expressions that fit the situation, then write and revise their own sentences.

We create games with clear roles and goals, based on grammar from Synapse Core and conversations from Synapse Talk. Scenes and characters help students understand the situation and take part themselves.
In the website’s email-writing experience, you write first and can ask for hints if you get stuck. Compare your first and revised drafts to see what changed.
We are developing a way to record sentences written and answers chosen in games, so they can inform later practice and feedback.

Find a way of learning that suits you. We first ask why students are learning Korean and how they prefer to study. We consider their answers, revisions, and teacher observations together to understand their strengths and difficulties.
At the start, we ask about learning goals, the preferred order of explanations, when hints are needed, and how students want to receive feedback.
We distinguish what students tell us, actual learning records, and AI inferences. We do not judge personality or ability from a single choice or favorite character.
We are preparing settings that can change as goals or study preferences change. Students will be able to correct anything the app has misunderstood.

Tasks adapt to your learning record. We are developing an app that adjusts task topics, hints, and feedback to learners’ goals and records. It is designed to revisit difficult expressions and check whether students can use them without help.

We are preparing an approach that shows examples first to students who prefer them, and grammar explanations first to those who want the rule. On this website, you can write your own text, choose the hints you need, and compare your revision with your first draft.

We record first drafts, revisions, and hint use separately. The design lets teachers review AI summaries alongside the student’s actual circumstances and arrange further practice of difficult expressions in a new task.
We are developing an app that brings together mascot guidance, today’s task, feedback, and learning records. Practice informs the next task and its feedback.
Preparing a Korean patent application. Application planned for 2028.

Before class, a dance-trained instructor guides K-POP rhythm and basic movements. During class, learners connect movement with Korean expressions. After-class co-creation is an optional program for students who want to join. They choose a role in planning, scripting, performing, or editing, and can take part without performing or being filmed.

Students discuss what to make, listen to one another, explain their reasons in Korean, and check and revise ideas suggested by AI. Creating something together gives them practice in critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and responsible use of AI—skills they will need in an AI era.

Before class · K-POP warm-up with a professional instructor — An instructor who majored in dance demonstrates K-POP rhythms and basic movements and practices them with students. Activity intensity and duration are adjusted to students’ physical condition. Learners warm up to music they enjoy and catch their breath before joining Korean class.

During class · Connect movements with expressions — Connect words used in the activity, such as 돌다 (turn), 멈추다 (stop), and 함께 (together), with movements that express their meanings. In the fixed 30 minutes of group speaking within a 90-minute class, explain a sequence or make a suggestion such as 이 부분을 다시 해 볼까요? (Shall we try this part again?). Practice saying what you have learned, listening to the response, and explaining again.

After class · Optional co-creation — After-class co-creation is only for students who choose to join. Teams decide on a topic and format, then students choose roles in planning, scripting, performing, or editing. They can contribute through planning, writing, or editing without performing or being filmed. A dance-trained instructor guides students who choose choreography. Students listen to different views, ask why, explain their reasoning, and compare and revise ideas and wording suggested by AI. By explaining what they made together, they practise critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and communication in Korean.
Movement before learning, gestures that express word meanings, and activities that involve everyone. Explore the sources behind each idea and how LAB plans to use them.

Harvard Medical School · Naperville · Expert commentary · School practice
Harvard Medical School’s John Ratey explains the relationship between exercise, memory, and concentration. Naperville Central High School ran LRPE, placing physical activity before reading and mathematics classes.
In a Harvard Health interview, John Ratey explains that regular exercise may affect brain regions involved in memory and the neurotrophic factor BDNF. Naperville’s LRPE is a school example focused on this connection between physical activity and learning. A 2013 Illinois Public Health Institute case report describes physical education scheduled before reading and mathematics classes for students who needed learning support.
How LAB designs its classes: This informs our plans for K-POP rhythm and movement before class. We choose activities students can enjoy, then adjust duration and intensity by observing fatigue and participation in the lesson afterward.

Schools on the Move · Finland’s national program
Finland promoted Schools on the Move nationally to add movement during lessons and breaks. School staff reported benefits for learning and the school atmosphere.
Schools on the Move is a program with strategic leadership from Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture and National Agency for Education, and coordination by JAMK University of Applied Sciences. Rather than a single university experiment, it lets schools increase movement and student participation in ways suited to their circumstances. Official program information and its interim report describe reducing prolonged sitting and involving students in planning activities.
How LAB designs its classes: We connect movement before class with Korean lessons, while preparing after-class co-creation as an optional activity. Roles beyond dance include planning, scripting, and editing, so students can practise listening to and resolving different views.

Max Planck Institute · Vocabulary research in cognitive and brain science
In a 2015 study, participants who performed gestures matching the meanings of unfamiliar words they heard remembered the words better. Meaningful pictures also helped memory.
Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences had participants learn unfamiliar words from an artificial language in several ways. Performing gestures or viewing pictures that matched the meanings helped vocabulary memory compared with listening alone. Watching a movement and performing it produced different results; the connection between the word’s meaning and the movement matters.
How LAB designs its classes: We choose gestures and images that fit the meanings of the Korean being learned. Students use the expressions to describe the order of movements or explain them to classmates, then use them again in cultural projects after class.

These sources inform LAB’s class design. They do not indicate partnerships or accreditation from these institutions, or verified results for LAB’s K-POP classes. LAB’s program is in preparation, and learning outcomes will be assessed during actual operation.

Is after-class co-creation required? — No. Only students who want to join take part in the after-class co-creation program. They can choose planning, scripting, comparing meanings, or editing without dancing, performing, or being filmed. Students decide whether to participate and which role they want.

Has research directly compared exercise and language learning? — A 2007 study by Winter and colleagues compared new vocabulary learning among 27 healthy participants after intense running, low-intensity running, and rest. We refer to it as experimental evidence that exercise conditions can affect vocabulary learning. LAB does not use it as proof of K-POP class outcomes or to claim the same improvement rate for every learner.
You can explore LAB even if you have not decided to study abroad. You can start by exploring a subject that interests you, life in Korea, or something you would like to do in Korean.

We chose Level 4 with university classes and daily life in mind. Building on Level 3 Korean, learners practice reading more complex materials and explaining their opinions.
TOPIK II PBT · Out of 300 — Level 3: 120–149 points / Level 4: 150–189 points
TOPIK II IBT · Out of 600 — Level 3: 191–290 points / Level 4: 291–360 points
What we practice at LAB — Level 3: Describe familiar situations and give reasons and opinions / Level 4: Compare sources and opinions, and explain academic and social topics
University classes and graduation — Practice reading and writing for academic work. We also review the requirements of universities that ask for Level 4 or higher at graduation.
Scholarship requirements — Some universities offer different scholarships for Levels 3 and 4. We help learners prepare by checking the actual requirements of their chosen universities.

Part-time work requirements by year — TOPIK Level 4 is the Korean-language standard for part-time work in the third and fourth years of a bachelor’s degree. Language requirements, work permission, and individual circumstances must all be checked.

Part-time work · Language standards and permitted hours by year — The Korean-language standard for part-time work is TOPIK Level 3 for first- and second-year undergraduates, and Level 4 for third- and fourth-year undergraduates. For third- and fourth-year students, the guidance allows 10 weekday hours without the language requirement and 25 hours with it. Preferential conditions, such as university accreditation or grades, may allow 30 hours. Alternatives to TOPIK are also recognized. Before starting work, students need confirmation from their university and immigration permission for part-time employment.

Scholarships · How Level 3 and Level 4 benefits differ — Konyang University’s tuition scholarship guidance for new and transfer students lists 30% for TOPIK Level 3 and 50% for Level 4—a difference of 20 percentage points at the same university. These benefits do not apply to every university. Check the latest admissions guide for the relevant semester, admissions track, and scholarship renewal conditions.

Graduation · Language requirements after admission — The Korean proficiency needed for admission may differ from that required for graduation. For example, Sangmyung University lists TOPIK Level 4 or higher for Korean graduation certification in general academic fields. Requirements and accepted alternatives vary by university, department, and admission year. LAB chose Level 4 as a goal that looks beyond admission.

Work and visas · Language credentials and workplace preparation — TOPIK results can serve as evidence of Korean proficiency in employment and immigration reviews. Alongside Level 4 preparation, we plan practice in explaining experience at interviews and clarifying workplace tasks. Job-seeking status (D-10) and employment status (such as E-7) are different categories, with separate requirements for education, occupation, contracts, and more. Level 4 alone does not secure a work visa or resolve immigration matters.

Official guidance checked on September 18, 2026. The scores above are for TOPIK II; the speaking test is separate. The practice activities described are LAB’s curriculum design. A TOPIK level alone does not measure all speaking or workplace skills. Part-time work, scholarships, graduation, and immigration requirements vary by person and institution. Passing TOPIK is not guaranteed.

LAB aims to prepare learners for studying in Korea and for life beyond it. TOPIK Level 4 is a clear goal, supported by experience using Korean in real situations. We want to help learners use AI while developing the ability to explain their own thinking and evaluate the results.

We are currently developing the curriculum, textbooks, and student app as we prepare to open. Participation requirements and schedules will be announced separately for each program. Learners remain responsible for choosing and changing their own direction. Learning outcomes are not guaranteed.
LAB develops textbooks, games, and a learning app together. We design them so students can use what they learn in practice and teachers can refer to that process to provide the help they need.
Textbooks and games — Practice grammar learned in Synapse Core through Synapse Talk conversations and scenario-based games. Tasks have clear purposes, such as making a request or sharing an opinion.
Learning records and feedback — First drafts, revisions, and hint use are recorded separately. Teachers are intended to review AI summaries alongside the student’s actual circumstances.

A next task suited to each learner — Learning goals and records inform adjustments to task topics, the order of explanations, and hints. We are preparing opportunities to practice difficult expressions again in a different situation.

The manuscripts for six Synapse Core grammar books and two Synapse Talk conversation books are complete, and we are preparing for publication. Games and a learning app for practicing class material are also in development.
Eight textbooks — Connect understanding grammar with speaking and writing practice. Core covers material through Level 5 and Talk through Level 4.
Games and learning records — Use Korean in tasks with roles and goals, and compare your first draft with feedback. You can try email writing on the website.

Personalized learning app — We are developing one place to see tasks, hints, feedback, and learning records. It is designed to reflect changes in learning goals and preferred approaches in subsequent learning.

Explain your study goals in a visa interview, ask for help at university, and describe your experience in a job interview. We are preparing VR learning that lets students practice situations they may face in real life.

Visa interview practice — We are preparing mock interviews within the one-year curriculum to help students organize their study goals and plans and answer questions. The aim is to explain their own plans clearly, rather than memorize answers.

Life in Korea and workplace experiences — Practice asking questions at university, clarifying work instructions, reporting problems, and requesting help. We also prepare job interview practice for explaining application reasons and experience.

How is a visa interview different from entry screening? — A visa interview may be requested by an overseas diplomatic mission during visa assessment. Entry screening is a separate process on arrival in Korea. LAB is preparing educational activities and mock practice to help learners explain their study goals and plans. This is not a visa application agency service or a guarantee of approval. Check the relevant diplomatic mission’s guidance for interview requirements and documents.
VR interview and workplace experiences are in preparation and are not yet formally offered. Activity records do not represent actual work experience or official qualifications.

Work toward TOPIK Level 4 while gaining experience for studying and living in Korea. Every 90-minute class includes a fixed 30 minutes of group speaking, connected with games, cultural activities, and personalized learning.

Korean for TOPIK Level 4 — Study grammar, listening, reading, and writing step by step, then use what you learn in conversations and scenario-based games. Practice both test formats and real communication.

Judgment and teamwork in the AI age — Choose a topic that reflects your interests and values, then develop a team project. Practice checking AI suggestions, listening to different views, finding agreement, and explaining your choices.

A portfolio for studying abroad — Organize your self-introduction, study plan, original and revised writing, presentation materials, and team roles. These materials help you prepare for classes and daily life in Korea and explain your experience.

Visa interviews and life in Korea — We are preparing mock interviews within the one-year program so learners can explain their study goals and plans in their own words. VR activities are designed to let learners experience interviews and unfamiliar daily situations, then practice difficult expressions again.

From the basics to Level 4: the learning stages — Build the foundations — Learn Hangul and basic sentence patterns, then speak and write in common situations such as introductions, ordering, and making plans. We also review each learner’s goals and current level.

Explain reasons and opinions — Add reasons to your ideas and check your understanding of others. Use what you learn in academic and everyday situations, such as making requests to professors and sharing ideas in team assignments.

Prepare for Level 4 and studying abroad — Practice listening, reading, and writing formats while comparing sources and organizing opinions. Presentations, interviews, and collaborative tasks connect test preparation with experience explaining ideas in practice.

Online learning support after the program — If you do not reach Level 4 on your first TOPIK test after the one-year program, we extend your academy app account free for six months to support online learning. Attendance or homework shortfalls do not disqualify you from this support. This is not an indefinite extension of in-person classes or a guarantee of passing.

Textbooks, games, and teachers work toward the same learning goals — The two Synapse Talk conversation books cover material through Level 4, and the six Synapse Core grammar books through Level 5. Level 4 is the main learning goal, not the limit of the textbooks. We are preparing a process in which students use textbook expressions in games, and teachers review their answers and revisions to plan further practice. Personalization aims to distinguish what learners already know from what needs more practice, so their time goes where it is needed.

What conversation, English, and cultural activities include — Programs that include native Korean conversation and global English offer practice in introductions, questions, presentations, and understanding materials in both languages. K-POP and cultural activities provide opportunities to plan together and coordinate roles. The scope of conversation and English classes depends on the enrolled program. Schedules and conditions will be available in enrollment information.

Preparing for life and work in Korea — At LAB, learners study Korean, practice real situations, and organize learning and project work into a portfolio. Those who need more support with settling in Korea or finding work after graduation can ask about separate PATH services. PATH is preparing guidance and connections with schools and employers based on each learner’s intended major and career. LAB enrollment does not include every PATH service or guarantee admission or employment.

We are preparing to open and developing the curriculum, app, and VR program. TOPIK Level 4 is the program’s goal, not a guaranteed outcome. The portfolio documents work completed by the student; it does not replace official language scores or qualifications.
Learning to decide what to create and whom to create it for, rather than simply following AI output. We help learners use their values to guide choices, work with others, and review the results.

Values and philosophy · Find what guides your choices — Ask what kind of life you want and how you want to help others. When starting a project, choose its audience and purpose yourself. Practice respecting others’ choices while considering how your own ideas may affect them.

Creativity · Find ideas in your experience — Find topics in the culture you enjoy and difficulties you have experienced. Explore several approaches and make a small first draft. Compare AI suggestions, add your own experience and expression, and explain what you made different.

Cooperation and consideration · Understand each other’s roles — In crew activities, share roles such as planning, writing, performing, and editing. Ask what classmates find difficult and adjust participation and schedules together. Activities provide experience in doing your part and giving and receiving help.

Openness · Listen to other views and reconsider — When opinions differ, hear the other person’s reasons first. Decide which feedback to use and which choices to keep, with reasons. We encourage learners to try new approaches and revise their thinking when they find a stronger reason.

Judgment · Check AI suggestions and make a choice — Learn the basics of how AI works and its limits, and check its answers against source material. Compare your own draft with AI suggestions and choose what to use or revise. Also learn the responsibilities involved in handling personal information and other people’s creative work.

Expression · Explain your work and your reasons — Explain in Korean whom you created the work for, your role, and the choices you made. Listen and respond to questions after presenting. Organize both the finished work and revisions to show your interests and abilities through specific examples.

Why Korean and foundational learning still matter in the AI age — You need to read and understand sources to review AI answers, and express your own thinking to work with others. LAB connects discussion, writing, and cultural projects with Korean study for TOPIK Level 4. We design classes that distinguish trying independently, receiving necessary help, and explaining again without help, to see what students have actually learned.

Which sources inform this approach? · Checked September 18, 2026 — WEF’s 2025 employer survey highlights analytical and creative thinking, flexibility, self-awareness, and lifelong learning. UNESCO’s 2024 AI competency framework for students and the OECD–European Union’s 2026 AI literacy framework address human-centered judgment, creativity, collaboration, and responsible use. The OECD’s 2026 education outlook emphasizes that performing well on a task with AI is not the same as learning. LAB draws on these sources and its own educational philosophy to design the classes below. These sources do not demonstrate LAB’s educational outcomes or imply institutional accreditation.
Talk directly with native Korean teachers and use expressions learned in your textbooks. Refine your pronunciation and polite language, and practice answering unexpected questions in your own words.
English classes cover introductions and everyday conversation, then reading, emails, and presentations. We assess Korean and English separately to prepare classes suited to each learner’s level.

Native Korean conversation — Practice making requests, asking questions, and sharing opinions with a native Korean teacher. The teacher identifies points to improve in pronunciation, intonation, and polite language, and helps you express your meaning clearly. You use textbook grammar in conversation and learn which expressions fit the situation.

For example, you ask a professor for a meeting, learn that the time is unavailable, and suggest another time. When the teacher changes a question or condition, you adjust your response. After the conversation, review what was clear and what needs work, then try again. Practice the Korean needed to ask questions at university and request help in everyday life.

English classes — Start by introducing yourself and answering questions in English. Learners who need the basics listen to and say short sentences, then move on to reading in their field of interest, writing emails, presentations, and team activities. Lessons cover checking information and explaining opinions at school or work.

For example, write a message introducing a team project to an exchange student and answer questions about roles and schedules. With the teacher, add missing information and revise awkward expressions, then respond to a changed schedule or condition. The length of materials, difficulty of questions, and amount of explanation are adjusted to the learner’s English level and goals.

What if my Korean and English levels are different? — We assess Korean and English separately. If you are comfortable speaking Korean but new to English, for example, English classes begin with basic expressions. In each class, we review what learners say and write and prepare further practice for difficult pronunciation or expressions. Learners then try the same expressions in a different situation to check their understanding.

Which programs include these classes? — We are preparing a program focused on regular Korean classes and another that also includes native Korean conversation and English. Students who want conversation and English classes can choose a program that includes them. Check enrollment information or ask us about opening dates, teachers, class frequency, and what is included.

How does this support TOPIK, studying abroad, and career preparation? — TOPIK · Put what you understand into speech and writing — Use vocabulary and grammar from Korean classes to answer a native teacher’s questions and explain your opinions. Write up the conversation afterward to compare spoken expressions with the written style used in test answers. Listening, reading, and writing are also practiced separately in the test formats.

Studying abroad · Ask questions, get help, and take part — Practice asking professors questions, agreeing on roles in team assignments, and checking information at university offices in Korean. English tasks include explaining opinions to international peers and reading short materials in your field or instructions for English-taught classes. Practice asking again and checking anything you did not understand.

Career preparation · Explain experience and clarify work — Describe your project role and the problems you solved in Korean, then answer follow-up interview questions. Students preparing for careers that require English also practice introductions, work emails, summaries, and short presentations. Beyond rehearsing answers, tasks include asking about unclear instructions and confirming schedules and results.

What will students take away? — We aim to help students build a portfolio of Korean request emails and opinion pieces they have written and revised, Korean and English introductions and project descriptions, expressions refined through teacher feedback, team roles, and presentation materials. Recording original wording alongside the reasons for revisions helps students explain their progress. Teachers use this work to suggest further practice, and students can revisit useful materials before a new semester or interview. The length and difficulty of the work depend on the student’s starting level and chosen program.

How are both languages used in one project? — For example, in a project creating a university guide for new international students, learners ask the university questions in Korean and organize the information they confirm. With an English teacher, they identify useful information in English guides and write a message for students from other countries. With a native Korean teacher, they explain the guide aloud and answer unexpected questions. Students compare AI translations or drafts with verified sources and explain why they chose the final wording.

Do English and native-speaker conversation help with TOPIK? — TOPIK II assesses Korean listening, reading, and writing; speaking is a separate test. We design listening, reading, and writing tasks that revisit vocabulary and expressions used in conversation to support test study. English is not assessed in TOPIK. LAB’s English classes aim to help learners understand English materials and communicate in another language; we do not claim that English classes themselves raise TOPIK scores.

How do you check language requirements for study and work? — Korean-taught and English-taught university programs may require different evidence of language proficiency. We first check the latest requirements of the chosen university and department, then distinguish preparation for official tests from practice needed to participate in classes. Career tasks are also based on the languages required by the intended role and job listing. Work completed in LAB classes does not replace official language scores or guarantee admission or employment.

Native Korean conversation and English classes are in preparation. The situations above are sample class activities. Opening dates and what each program includes will be available in enrollment information.

LAB prepares learners for both language qualifications and real communication. We broaden practice situations so students can organize what they learn into test answers, talk with professors, and explain their experience in interviews. Our English teaching aims to help students read materials and collaborate in ways relevant to their intended major and career.

TOPIK · Put what you understand into speech and writing — Use vocabulary and grammar from Korean classes to answer a native teacher’s questions and explain your opinions. Write up the conversation afterward to compare spoken expressions with the written style used in test answers. Listening, reading, and writing are also practiced separately in the test formats.
Set your goals in Compass, then plan and create with others in crew projects. Teachers observe the work and conversations to provide feedback, and students record their revisions in a portfolio.

Set your goal with Compass — Talk about why you are learning Korean and what kind of life you want. Every eight-week season, choose a challenge and reflect on it. Your first answer is not fixed as the correct one. If your goal changes through experience, record why it changed.

Plan and finish a project with your crew — Use cultural activities to decide what your team wants to share and with whom. Divide the roles, create a draft, and review each other’s work along the way. Projects are designed so students make real decisions within their roles and see their work through to completion.

Use feedback and try again — Teachers review students’ questions, conversations about roles, and revisions. Together with students’ self-assessments, these help identify what support is needed next. Practice might begin with short explanations when presenting is difficult, or comparing sources when evidence is lacking.

Show your choices and growth in a portfolio — Alongside the finished work, organize your original goal, your own draft, your role, and the reasons for revisions. Prepare materials that let you explain, in your own words, what matters to you and what you have tried. Reflect on them when choosing a goal for the next season.

Sample cultural project · Introducing K-culture to a newcomer — Choose music, food, or a game as a team and ask what someone encountering it for the first time might want to know. Decide whether to use a performance, introduction video, or short guide, and write the Korean script yourselves. A team that values everyone’s participation, for example, can make roles for classmates who find dancing difficult. Coordinate schedules and roles, check AI wording suggestions, sources, and usage terms, then revise in response to each other’s reactions. In the presentation, explain why you chose the topic and format and what you changed. This sample activity connects the enjoyment of culture with choices that reflect consideration and values.

How do personalized learning and teachers work together? — We are developing a way to adjust support and the next task by considering the student’s stated goals, completed tasks, and teacher observations together. We do not judge personality from a single activity or score personal values. The website’s email-writing experience shows how guidance can change based on goals, available time, preferred support, and responses after the activity. Automatically connecting classroom observations with all tasks, carrying learning records across devices, and collecting portfolio materials automatically remain development work.

What experience do you want students to leave with? — The experience of expressing an opinion, listening to others, and completing something together. We want to help learners choose their roles and the support they need more specifically in their next project. For LAB, leadership means setting your own direction while collaborating responsibly with others. We support students in finding reasons for their choices, without choosing their interests or careers for them.

The program connecting Compass, crew projects, and portfolios is in preparation. The project above is an example of class design, not a record of actual student performance or measured skill improvement.

Form your own view, listen to classmates’ reasons, and coordinate what you will do together. Classes are designed to help learners consider others while making and explaining their own final decisions.

Start with your own view — Each learner prepares an opinion on the same situation or task. Decide what you would choose and why, then share it with the group. This is practice in forming your own judgment before hearing other people’s answers.

Listen and find agreement — Take turns speaking and ask again when something is unclear. When opinions differ, listen to the reasons and discuss how everyone can participate. Practice expressing your ideas while considering others and working together.

Explain your decision and reasons — After the discussion, decide which parts of your original view to keep or change. Distinguish what the group agreed on from your own judgment, and explain your reasons. The teacher helps with expressions while guiding students to find and explain their own reasons.

How are the 30 minutes used? — This is group activity time within the 90-minute class. It is not an extra 30 minutes or 30 minutes of solo speaking per student. Learners practice speaking, listening, asking questions, and coordinating, while the teacher checks that the conversation is not dominated by a few students. Task difficulty and support are adjusted to the learners’ levels, while the group speaking time remains fixed.
These are operating guidelines for the regular classes currently in preparation. Cooperation, consideration, and judgment are skills we aim to develop, not measured improvement results.

docs.title: SYNK — Our philosophy
paragraphs: SYNK builds personalized systems. We develop technology that understands each person's goals, circumstances, and experience and provides the support they need. As their goals and needs change, the system is designed to change with them.
Five principles guide how SYNK works.

Understand the person first — We consider each person's goals, current circumstances, strengths, and difficulties. We build systems that use this understanding to suggest relevant learning and support.

Support that fits changing needs — We look beyond the first assessment and take later experiences and choices into account. When goals change or new difficulties arise, learning content and support change too.
Easy to use from the start — We make it easy to find the right features and understand what to do next. We refine every step, from the layout and instructions to the end of the experience.

Keep student work and AI edits distinct — We preserve students' own answers and teachers' observations as original records. AI revisions and inferences are labeled separately so people can review the basis for learning decisions and correct misinterpretations.

Less repetition, more time to learn — Technology helps organize materials and handle repetitive work so people can focus on learning, conversation, and cultural experiences. We want working toward a goal to include the enjoyment of learning and doing things together.
These principles guide the education, services, and content we are preparing. We distinguish plans from current operations. Each brand's page explains what is available now.

We check whether explanations are clear, interfaces are easy to use, and the promised features work properly. Our published production guides let you compare the original work with the revised result.
We use AI to help with repetitive recording, organization, and production. People understand one another, build relationships, and make important decisions.

When students change their goals or preferences, their education should be able to reflect that. We record what students say, what teachers observe, and what AI infers as distinct types of information.
We distinguish between what is planned, what has been built, what is actually in use, and what has demonstrated results.

We compare schools' application requirements based on your intended major and career after graduation, then map out your preparation schedule. Taking your current Korean level and available study time into account, we guide you step by step through language learning, application documents, and interview practice.

Practice Korean for real situations — When asking a professor a question or explaining your motivation in an interview, you need to put your Korean into use. The approach is to try expressions learned at LAB in VR situations, then practice difficult expressions again in class.

Update the plan as your goals change — Exploring a major or role may spark an interest in another field, or learning Korean may take longer than expected. We review what you want to change and your current progress, then adjust your school choices, learning plan, and preparation schedule.

Explain your study plans in a visa interview, ask questions in a university class, or discuss your experience in a job interview. Answering questions yourself helps reveal difficult expressions and what you still need to prepare. We are developing VR education so you can combine this practice with LAB's Korean lessons.

Visa interview — Listen and respond to questions about why you want to study in Korea, your intended major, and your future plans. Note any ideas or expressions that were hard to explain, then practice them again.

University classes and everyday life — Practice asking about something you did not understand in class, speaking with a professor, and requesting information at a university office. Learn how to ask again when you have not understood the other person.

Explore roles and practice job interviews — Explore the work involved in a role that interests you, then practice explaining your motivation and relevant experience in an interview. Afterwards, note what you want to learn more about and what was difficult to inform career guidance and job preparation.

Before class, a dance-trained instructor guides K-POP rhythm and basic movements. During class, learners connect movement with Korean expressions. After-class co-creation is an optional program for students who want to join. They choose a role in planning, scripting, performing, or editing, and can take part without performing or being filmed.

Students discuss what to make, listen to one another, explain their reasons in Korean, and check and revise ideas suggested by AI. Creating something together gives them practice in critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and responsible use of AI—skills they will need in an AI era.

Before class · K-POP warm-up with a professional instructor — An instructor who majored in dance demonstrates K-POP rhythms and basic movements and practices them with students. Activity intensity and duration are adjusted to students’ physical condition. Learners warm up to music they enjoy and catch their breath before joining Korean class.

During class · Connect movements with expressions — Connect words used in the activity, such as 돌다 (turn), 멈추다 (stop), and 함께 (together), with movements that express their meanings. In the fixed 30 minutes of group speaking within a 90-minute class, explain a sequence or make a suggestion such as 이 부분을 다시 해 볼까요? (Shall we try this part again?). Practice saying what you have learned, listening to the response, and explaining again.

After class · Optional co-creation — After-class co-creation is only for students who choose to join. Teams decide on a topic and format, then students choose roles in planning, scripting, performing, or editing. They can contribute through planning, writing, or editing without performing or being filmed. A dance-trained instructor guides students who choose choreography. Students listen to different views, ask why, explain their reasoning, and compare and revise ideas and wording suggested by AI. By explaining what they made together, they practise critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and communication in Korean.

Movement before learning, gestures that express word meanings, and activities that involve everyone. Explore the sources behind each idea and how LAB plans to use them.

Harvard Medical School · Naperville · Expert commentary · School practice
Harvard Medical School’s John Ratey explains the relationship between exercise, memory, and concentration. Naperville Central High School ran LRPE, placing physical activity before reading and mathematics classes.
In a Harvard Health interview, John Ratey explains that regular exercise may affect brain regions involved in memory and the neurotrophic factor BDNF. Naperville’s LRPE is a school example focused on this connection between physical activity and learning. A 2013 Illinois Public Health Institute case report describes physical education scheduled before reading and mathematics classes for students who needed learning support.
How LAB designs its classes: This informs our plans for K-POP rhythm and movement before class. We choose activities students can enjoy, then adjust duration and intensity by observing fatigue and participation in the lesson afterward.

Schools on the Move · Finland’s national program
Finland promoted Schools on the Move nationally to add movement during lessons and breaks. School staff reported benefits for learning and the school atmosphere.
Schools on the Move is a program with strategic leadership from Finland’s Ministry of Education and Culture and National Agency for Education, and coordination by JAMK University of Applied Sciences. Rather than a single university experiment, it lets schools increase movement and student participation in ways suited to their circumstances. Official program information and its interim report describe reducing prolonged sitting and involving students in planning activities.
How LAB designs its classes: We connect movement before class with Korean lessons, while preparing after-class co-creation as an optional activity. Roles beyond dance include planning, scripting, and editing, so students can practise listening to and resolving different views.

Max Planck Institute · Vocabulary research in cognitive and brain science
In a 2015 study, participants who performed gestures matching the meanings of unfamiliar words they heard remembered the words better. Meaningful pictures also helped memory.
Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences had participants learn unfamiliar words from an artificial language in several ways. Performing gestures or viewing pictures that matched the meanings helped vocabulary memory compared with listening alone. Watching a movement and performing it produced different results; the connection between the word’s meaning and the movement matters.
How LAB designs its classes: We choose gestures and images that fit the meanings of the Korean being learned. Students use the expressions to describe the order of movements or explain them to classmates, then use them again in cultural projects after class.

These sources inform LAB’s class design. They do not indicate partnerships or accreditation from these institutions, or verified results for LAB’s K-POP classes. LAB’s program is in preparation, and learning outcomes will be assessed during actual operation.

Is after-class co-creation required? — No. Only students who want to join take part in the after-class co-creation program. They can choose planning, scripting, comparing meanings, or editing without dancing, performing, or being filmed. Students decide whether to participate and which role they want.

Has research directly compared exercise and language learning? — A 2007 study by Winter and colleagues compared new vocabulary learning among 27 healthy participants after intense running, low-intensity running, and rest. We refer to it as experimental evidence that exercise conditions can affect vocabulary learning. LAB does not use it as proof of K-POP class outcomes or to claim the same improvement rate for every learner.

Support that fits changing needs — We look beyond the first assessment and take later experiences and choices into account. When goals change or new difficulties arise, learning content and support change too.

Easy to use from the start — We make it easy to find the right features and understand what to do next. We refine every step, from the layout and instructions to the end of the experience.

Keep student work and AI edits distinct — We preserve students' own answers and teachers' observations as original records. AI revisions and inferences are labeled separately so people can review the basis for learning decisions and correct misinterpretations.

Less repetition, more time to learn — Technology helps organize materials and handle repetitive work so people can focus on learning, conversation, and cultural experiences. We want working toward a goal to include the enjoyment of learning and doing things together.

These principles guide the education, services, and content we are preparing. We distinguish plans from current operations. Each brand's page explains what is available now.

records.title: Why does LAB aim for Level 4?
records.answer:
We chose Level 4 with university classes and daily life in mind. Building on Level 3 Korean, learners practice reading more complex materials and explaining their opinions.

TOPIK II PBT · Out of 300 — Level 3: 120–149 points / Level 4: 150–189 points

TOPIK II IBT · Out of 600 — Level 3: 191–290 points / Level 4: 291–360 points

What we practice at LAB — Level 3: Describe familiar situations and give reasons and opinions / Level 4: Compare sources and opinions, and explain academic and social topics

University classes and graduation — Practice reading and writing for academic work. We also review the requirements of universities that ask for Level 4 or higher at graduation.

Scholarship requirements — Some universities offer different scholarships for Levels 3 and 4. We help learners prepare by checking the actual requirements of their chosen universities.

Part-time work requirements by year — TOPIK Level 4 is the Korean-language standard for part-time work in the third and fourth years of a bachelor’s degree. Language requirements, work permission, and individual circumstances must all be checked.

Part-time work · Language standards and permitted hours by year — The Korean-language standard for part-time work is TOPIK Level 3 for first- and second-year undergraduates, and Level 4 for third- and fourth-year undergraduates. For third- and fourth-year students, the guidance allows 10 weekday hours without the language requirement and 25 hours with it. Preferential conditions, such as university accreditation or grades, may allow 30 hours. Alternatives to TOPIK are also recognized. Before starting work, students need confirmation from their university and immigration permission for part-time employment.

Scholarships · How Level 3 and Level 4 benefits differ — Konyang University’s tuition scholarship guidance for new and transfer students lists 30% for TOPIK Level 3 and 50% for Level 4—a difference of 20 percentage points at the same university. These benefits do not apply to every university. Check the latest admissions guide for the relevant semester, admissions track, and scholarship renewal conditions.

Graduation · Language requirements after admission — The Korean proficiency needed for admission may differ from that required for graduation. For example, Sangmyung University lists TOPIK Level 4 or higher for Korean graduation certification in general academic fields. Requirements and accepted alternatives vary by university, department, and admission year. LAB chose Level 4 as a goal that looks beyond admission.

Work and visas · Language credentials and workplace preparation — TOPIK results can serve as evidence of Korean proficiency in employment and immigration reviews. Alongside Level 4 preparation, we plan practice in explaining experience at interviews and clarifying workplace tasks. Job-seeking status (D-10) and employment status (such as E-7) are different categories, with separate requirements for education, occupation, contracts, and more. Level 4 alone does not secure a work visa or resolve immigration matters.

Official guidance checked on September 18, 2026. The scores above are for TOPIK II; the speaking test is separate. The practice activities described are LAB’s curriculum design. A TOPIK level alone does not measure all speaking or workplace skills. Part-time work, scholarships, graduation, and immigration requirements vary by person and institution. Passing TOPIK is not guaranteed.

records.answer:
Learning to decide what to create and whom to create it for, rather than simply following AI output. We help learners use their values to guide choices, work with others, and review the results.

Values and philosophy · Find what guides your choices — Ask what kind of life you want and how you want to help others. When starting a project, choose its audience and purpose yourself. Practice respecting others’ choices while considering how your own ideas may affect them.

Creativity · Find ideas in your experience — Find topics in the culture you enjoy and difficulties you have experienced. Explore several approaches and make a small first draft. Compare AI suggestions, add your own experience and expression, and explain what you made different.

Cooperation and consideration · Understand each other’s roles — In crew activities, share roles such as planning, writing, performing, and editing. Ask what classmates find difficult and adjust participation and schedules together. Activities provide experience in doing your part and giving and receiving help.

Openness · Listen to other views and reconsider — When opinions differ, hear the other person’s reasons first. Decide which feedback to use and which choices to keep, with reasons. We encourage learners to try new approaches and revise their thinking when they find a stronger reason.

Judgment · Check AI suggestions and make a choice — Learn the basics of how AI works and its limits, and check its answers against source material. Compare your own draft with AI suggestions and choose what to use or revise. Also learn the responsibilities involved in handling personal information and other people’s creative work.

Expression · Explain your work and your reasons — Explain in Korean whom you created the work for, your role, and the choices you made. Listen and respond to questions after presenting. Organize both the finished work and revisions to show your interests and abilities through specific examples.

Why Korean and foundational learning still matter in the AI age — You need to read and understand sources to review AI answers, and express your own thinking to work with others. LAB connects discussion, writing, and cultural projects with Korean study for TOPIK Level 4. We design classes that distinguish trying independently, receiving necessary help, and explaining again without help, to see what students have actually learned.

records.answer:
Talk directly with native Korean teachers and use expressions learned in your textbooks. Refine your pronunciation and polite language, and practice answering unexpected questions in your own words.

English classes cover introductions and everyday conversation, then reading, emails, and presentations. We assess Korean and English separately to prepare classes suited to each learner’s level.

Native Korean conversation — Practice making requests, asking questions, and sharing opinions with a native Korean teacher. The teacher identifies points to improve in pronunciation, intonation, and polite language, and helps you express your meaning clearly. You use textbook grammar in conversation and learn which expressions fit the situation.

For example, you ask a professor for a meeting, learn that the time is unavailable, and suggest another time. When the teacher changes a question or condition, you adjust your response. After the conversation, review what was clear and what needs work, then try again. Practice the Korean needed to ask questions at university and request help in everyday life.

English classes — Start by introducing yourself and answering questions in English. Learners who need the basics listen to and say short sentences, then move on to reading in their field of interest, writing emails, presentations, and team activities. Lessons cover checking information and explaining opinions at school or work.

For example, write a message introducing a team project to an exchange student and answer questions about roles and schedules. With the teacher, add missing information and revise awkward expressions, then respond to a changed schedule or condition. The length of materials, difficulty of questions, and amount of explanation are adjusted to the learner’s English level and goals.

What if my Korean and English levels are different? — We assess Korean and English separately. If you are comfortable speaking Korean but new to English, for example, English classes begin with basic expressions. In each class, we review what learners say and write and prepare further practice for difficult pronunciation or expressions. Learners then try the same expressions in a different situation to check their understanding.

Which programs include these classes? — We are preparing a program focused on regular Korean classes and another that also includes native Korean conversation and English. Students who want conversation and English classes can choose a program that includes them. Check enrollment information or ask us about opening dates, teachers, class frequency, and what is included.

How does this support TOPIK, studying abroad, and career preparation? — TOPIK · Put what you understand into speech and writing — Use vocabulary and grammar from Korean classes to answer a native teacher’s questions and explain your opinions. Write up the conversation afterward to compare spoken expressions with the written style used in test answers. Listening, reading, and writing are also practiced separately in the test formats.

Studying abroad · Ask questions, get help, and take part — Practice asking professors questions, agreeing on roles in team assignments, and checking information at university offices in Korean. English tasks include explaining opinions to international peers and reading short materials in your field or instructions for English-taught classes. Practice asking again and checking anything you did not understand.

Career preparation · Explain experience and clarify work — Describe your project role and the problems you solved in Korean, then answer follow-up interview questions. Students preparing for careers that require English also practice introductions, work emails, summaries, and short presentations. Beyond rehearsing answers, tasks include asking about unclear instructions and confirming schedules and results.

What will students take away? — We aim to help students build a portfolio of Korean request emails and opinion pieces they have written and revised, Korean and English introductions and project descriptions, expressions refined through teacher feedback, team roles, and presentation materials. Recording original wording alongside the reasons for revisions helps students explain their progress. Teachers use this work to suggest further practice, and students can revisit useful materials before a new semester or interview. The length and difficulty of the work depend on the student’s starting level and chosen program.

How are both languages used in one project? — For example, in a project creating a university guide for new international students, learners ask the university questions in Korean and organize the information they confirm. With an English teacher, they identify useful information in English guides and write a message for students from other countries. With a native Korean teacher, they explain the guide aloud and answer unexpected questions. Students compare AI translations or drafts with verified sources and explain why they chose the final wording.

Do English and native-speaker conversation help with TOPIK? — TOPIK II assesses Korean listening, reading, and writing; speaking is a separate test. We design listening, reading, and writing tasks that revisit vocabulary and expressions used in conversation to support test study. English is not assessed in TOPIK. LAB’s English classes aim to help learners understand English materials and communicate in another language; we do not claim that English classes themselves raise TOPIK scores.

How do you check language requirements for study and work? — Korean-taught and English-taught university programs may require different evidence of language proficiency. We first check the latest requirements of the chosen university and department, then distinguish preparation for official tests from practice needed to participate in classes. Career tasks are also based on the languages required by the intended role and job listing. Work completed in LAB classes does not replace official language scores or guarantee admission or employment.

Native Korean conversation and English classes are in preparation. The situations above are sample class activities. Opening dates and what each program includes will be available in enrollment information.

We first check the latest requirements of the chosen university and department, then distinguish preparation for official tests from practice needed to participate in classes. Career tasks are also based on the languages required by the intended role and job listing. Work completed in LAB classes does not replace official language scores or guarantee admission or employment.

records.title: How do LAB’s Compass and crew projects connect?
keywords: Plan and finish a project with your crew
Show your choices and growth in a portfolio
Sample cultural project · Introducing K-culture to a newcomer
How do personalized learning and teachers work together?
What experience do you want students to leave with?
questionExamples: How do LAB’s Compass and crew projects connect?
How do cultural activities teach cooperation and consideration?
What materials do students take away from LAB’s projects?
records.answer:
Set your goals in Compass, then plan and create with others in crew projects. Teachers observe the work and conversations to provide feedback, and students record their revisions in a portfolio.

Set your goal with Compass — Talk about why you are learning Korean and what kind of life you want. Every eight-week season, choose a challenge and reflect on it. Your first answer is not fixed as the correct one. If your goal changes through experience, record why it changed.

Plan and finish a project with your crew — Use cultural activities to decide what your team wants to share and with whom. Divide the roles, create a draft, and review each other’s work along the way. Projects are designed so students make real decisions within their roles and see their work through to completion.

Use feedback and try again — Teachers review students’ questions, conversations about roles, and revisions. Together with students’ self-assessments, these help identify what support is needed next. Practice might begin with short explanations when presenting is difficult, or comparing sources when evidence is lacking.

Show your choices and growth in a portfolio — Alongside the finished work, organize your original goal, your own draft, your role, and the reasons for revisions. Prepare materials that let you explain, in your own words, what matters to you and what you have tried. Reflect on them when choosing a goal for the next season.

Sample cultural project · Introducing K-culture to a newcomer — Choose music, food, or a game as a team and ask what someone encountering it for the first time might want to know. Decide whether to use a performance, introduction video, or short guide, and write the Korean script yourselves. A team that values everyone’s participation, for example, can make roles for classmates who find dancing difficult. Coordinate schedules and roles, check AI wording suggestions, sources, and usage terms, then revise in response to each other’s reactions. In the presentation, explain why you chose the topic and format and what you changed. This sample activity connects the enjoyment of culture with choices that reflect consideration and values.

How do personalized learning and teachers work together? — We are developing a way to adjust support and the next task by considering the student’s stated goals, completed tasks, and teacher observations together. We do not judge personality from a single activity or score personal values. The website’s email-writing experience shows how guidance can change based on goals, available time, preferred support, and responses after the activity. Automatically connecting classroom observations with all tasks, carrying learning records across devices, and collecting portfolio materials automatically remain development work.

What experience do you want students to leave with? — The experience of expressing an opinion, listening to others, and completing something together. We want to help learners choose their roles and the support they need more specifically in their next project. For LAB, leadership means setting your own direction while collaborating responsibly with others. We support students in finding reasons for their choices, without choosing their interests or careers for them.

The program connecting Compass, crew projects, and portfolios is in preparation. The project above is an example of class design, not a record of actual student performance or measured skill improvement.

records.title: How does a 90-minute LAB class work?
questionExamples: How does a 90-minute LAB class work?
What happens during the 30 minutes of group speaking?
Does a 90-minute class include 30 minutes of group work?
How much time does LAB allow for group speaking?
records.answer:
Form your own view, listen to classmates’ reasons, and coordinate what you will do together. Classes are designed to help learners consider others while making and explaining their own final decisions.

Start with your own view — Each learner prepares an opinion on the same situation or task. Decide what you would choose and why, then share it with the group. This is practice in forming your own judgment before hearing other people’s answers.

Listen and find agreement — Take turns speaking and ask again when something is unclear. When opinions differ, listen to the reasons and discuss how everyone can participate. Practice expressing your ideas while considering others and working together.

Explain your decision and reasons — After the discussion, decide which parts of your original view to keep or change. Distinguish what the group agreed on from your own judgment, and explain your reasons. The teacher helps with expressions while guiding students to find and explain their own reasons.

How are the 30 minutes used? — This is group activity time within the 90-minute class. It is not an extra 30 minutes or 30 minutes of solo speaking per student. Learners practice speaking, listening, asking questions, and coordinating, while the teacher checks that the conversation is not dominated by a few students. Task difficulty and support are adjusted to the learners’ levels, while the group speaking time remains fixed.

These are operating guidelines for the regular classes currently in preparation. Cooperation, consideration, and judgment are skills we aim to develop, not measured improvement results.

records.title: How does SYNK Atlas work?
questionExamples: How does SYNK Atlas work?
What do the eight Atlas engines do?
How is Atlas used by each brand?
What does it mean for Atlas to evolve with the user?
records.answer:
Atlas is SYNK's core technology for finding the learning and support each person needs, based on their goals and experience. Eight engines share the work: understanding the person, choosing what to learn and in what order, explaining it, and reviewing the results.

A student may first prepare for university admission, then need help with presentations or job interviews while studying in Korea. We are developing Atlas to adjust tasks and explanations using the learner's new goals and recent work.

Core — Choosing the next learning step. Looks at what a learner wants to achieve and where they are struggling, then identifies the next task and the support they need.

Loom — Scenes that respond to you. Combines soft materials, light, and movement to create interfaces and characters, with scenes that respond naturally to the user's actions.

Vellum — Explanations that make sense. Offers explanations and hints suited to the current task and the student's answer. Explains why the practice matters and what to look at when the student gets stuck.

Trail — Tracking practice and progress. Records the tasks completed and the help received. Lets learners compare earlier and recent answers to see what has changed.

Prism — Comparing learning results. Finds recurring difficulties and differences across learning examples. Highlights which content and explanations need a closer look.

Temper — Checking whether support helped. Checks what actually changed after a hint or practice activity, then uses those results to improve tasks and support.

Reed — Music and sound for each scene. Handles music and sound for creative work and learning scenes. Adjusts their use around the listening experience and moments that need focus.

Strata (planned) — A map of what to learn next. Connects grammar, expressions, and vocabulary by difficulty and prerequisites. Helps identify the learning needed for a goal and which basics to revisit after a mistake.

lab.name: SYNK LAB
lab.headline: 개인 맞춤 한국어 교육을 설계하는 에듀테크 기업
lab.subtext: SYNK LAB은 한국어 교재와 게임, 개인화 학습 앱을 개발하는 에듀테크 기업입니다. TOPIK 4급을 목표로 하는 정규 오프라인 1년 과정과 한국인 원어민 회화·글로벌 영어 수업을 준비합니다. 문화체험과 AI 활용, 협업 과제까지 연결해 한국 유학과 이후의 삶을 준비하는 교육을 만듭니다.

shift.name: SYNK SHIFT
shift.headline: 기업과 기관을 위한 AI 교육과 브랜딩
shift.subtext: SYNK SHIFT는 기업·기관의 AI 강의와 실습, 업무 컨설팅, 기업 브랜딩을 준비합니다. 참여자의 경험과 실제 업무에 맞춰 교육과 제작 방법을 구성합니다.

pulse.name: SYNK PULSE
pulse.headline: 음악과 이야기로 만드는 콘텐츠와 IP
pulse.subtext: SYNK PULSE는 음악과 영상, 캐릭터와 이야기를 만듭니다. 온라인 콘텐츠와 자체 지식재산(IP)을 중심으로 작품 이용, 공동 제작, 광고 협업을 준비합니다.

path.name: SYNK PATH
path.headline: 한국 유학부터 취업까지, 함께 준비합니다.
path.subtext: SYNK PATH는 한국 유학을 준비하는 외국인을 위한 학업·생활·취업 지원 브랜드입니다. 학교 선택과 한국어 학습, 면접 준비부터 졸업 후 진로까지 함께 계획합니다. LAB의 한국어 교육과 VR 연습으로 한국에서 마주할 상황을 미리 경험하고, 준비한 내용을 포트폴리오로 정리하는 서비스를 준비하고 있습니다.
